userJob: Decide whether a sentence on the page is allowed to be there
problem: Delivery times, guarantees, capabilities and how the trade works are written because they read as helpful, and each of them is something a customer will hold the business to
worksWhen: Every sentence on every page, applied as a test rather than as a list of obvious cases
avoidWhen: Never; voice is yours to invent, facts are not
mechanism: If a reader could act on it, or hold the client to it, it is a claim. Ask that question of every sentence before it ships. The obvious cases are numbers, guarantees, delivery times, certifications and testimonials. The ones that get through are quieter: what the customer may do while they wait, what a document contains, what is enough to get started, and how the trade itself works. If it is not in the brief or the evidence it does not go on the page, not as a placeholder and not as a plausible example.
risks: Marking an invented sentence as a placeholder, which nobody replaces
Softening the claim into a vaguer sentence, which is the same claim with less to check
mobileRules: No mobile exception; a claim that only appears at one width is still a claim
accessibilityRules: A claim's supporting figure is text, not an image of text, so it can be read out and enlarged
genericnessNote: Cutting unsourced sentences removes the interchangeable marketing furniture that makes pages resemble each other.

userJob: Present evidence without making it sound stronger than it is
problem: A single figure is shown with no count and no spread, so a mean from three cases reads exactly like a mean from three hundred
worksWhen: Any performance figure, rating, benchmark, average or success rate
avoidWhen: A single measured fact about a single object, such as a dimension, where spread does not exist
mechanism: Proof carries its size, spread and worst cases. Show the distribution whole with its count rather than the headline value alone. Where proof is absent, name the absence and the reason for it, which is still an answer and is checkable.
risks: Showing a distribution but cropping its tail, which is curation wearing a chart
Rounding a small sample's mean to a precision the sample cannot support
mobileRules: A distribution at 375px usually needs a different chart, not the same chart scaled; state the count in text either way
accessibilityRules: Any chart carrying proof has a text alternative giving the count, the spread and the worst case
Do not rely on colour alone to separate series
genericnessNote: Real distributions differ per client, so showing them whole is the opposite of a reusable asset.

userJob: Judge whether a specific-looking number on the page is legitimate
problem: Precise-sounding figures are invented to make a page feel engineered, so the brand ends up claiming an accuracy it never measured
worksWhen: Any figure with decimals, units or a suspiciously specific value in copy, specifications or captions
avoidWhen: The figure comes from the brief, the brand guidelines or a public metric, where precision is earned
mechanism: Fake-precise numbers are flagged. A number either comes from real data, or is explicitly labelled as mock, or is banned. Don't fake engineering precision the brand doesn't claim.
risks: Labelling a figure as an example in a code comment where no reader sees it
Replacing a fake precise number with a fake round one, which is the same invention
accessibilityRules: Units are written out at least once rather than only implied by an abbreviation
genericnessNote: Removing invented specifications leaves the page carrying only what this client actually has.

userJob: Decide where each visual on the page comes from before writing any code
problem: Images are chosen while building, so licences are never recorded and a drawing gets used for a thing that could simply have been photographed
worksWhen: Every build, written as a table before the first line of code
avoidWhen: Never; a page with no assets still records that decision
mechanism: List every visual element with what it contributes, its source, its licence and its state. Climb the ladder from the top. First, supplied by the client, because a real photograph of the real thing beats anything you can make. Second, licensed and sourced, with the licence recorded before the file is used. Third, drawn here, which is the right answer for a thing that cannot be photographed and the wrong answer for a thing that exists.
risks: A photograph with no traceable licence used because it looks right
Drawing a schematic of an object that could have been photographed, which describes the subject instead of showing it
mobileRules: Each row records the aspect ratio it will occupy so the mobile stack reserves space rather than shifting
accessibilityRules: Each row records what its alt text will say, which forces the question of what the asset is doing there
A decorative asset is recorded as decorative rather than left to be guessed at markup time
genericnessNote: An asset plan tied to one client's own material cannot be carried to the next brief.

userJob: Handle a fact you tried to look up and could not find
problem: An empty search result quietly becomes a plausible fact, because the sentence still needs filling and the gap is invisible by the time anyone reviews the page
worksWhen: Any build that required looking something up: a specification, a regulation, a delivery window, a trade practice
avoidWhen: Never; the alternative is an unmarked invention
mechanism: A look-up that comes back empty does not become a plausible fact. It moves to the assumption pile, in those words, and appears in the report where a reader can challenge it. Assumptions are the evidence when there is no other evidence, which is only true if they are listed.
risks: Recording the assumption in a working note rather than in the report, so the client never sees it
Assuming something that changes what gets built, which should have been the run's one question instead
accessibilityRules: No accessibility-specific behaviour, but an assumed accessibility fact is the most expensive kind to leave unlisted
genericnessNote: An assumption list is per-brief by construction.

userJob: Show what the subject itself does not know, in the same form as what it does
problem: Unknowns are rounded, hidden or replaced by a placeholder value, so the page looks complete and the reader trusts a number nobody stands behind
worksWhen: The subject has real gaps in its own data: a sensor that stopped reporting, an index searched by hand, a route with no reading
avoidWhen: The gap is in the brief rather than in the subject, which belongs in the report and not on the page
mechanism: Set the subject's own unknown in the same form as the values it stands among, next to the value or the control it qualifies. A gauge silent since a stated time, with the sentence telling the reader what to do instead. A register searched by hand that takes three weeks, printed above the button rather than below it. A route with no reading named by number instead of shown as zero.
risks: Confusing the subject's unknown with the brief's gap, which files the studio's paperwork on the client's page
Setting the unknown in a smaller, quieter style, which is hiding it politely
mobileRules: The unknown keeps its adjacency to the value it qualifies after the columns collapse at 375px
accessibilityRules: An unknown is text in the same reading order as the values, not a tooltip or a title attribute
A silent instrument's state is announced as text rather than shown as a greyed-out figure
genericnessNote: An unknown belongs to one subject and cannot be transferred, which is why reviewers named it as what they trusted.

userJob: Test whether the design is carrying an argument or covering for one
problem: A layout is defended on composition while the text underneath does not persuade, so polish keeps being added to a page whose problem is what it says
worksWhen: Before defending any layout, and before a second correction round
avoidWhen: Never; the test costs one read
mechanism: Strip the page to its text and read what is left. If the words alone do not persuade, the design was carrying an empty page, and the fix is the argument rather than the layout. A second correction round is where a page gets sanded flat; if the second look is still wrong, the thesis was wrong and the report says so.
risks: Rewriting the copy to fit the layout instead of fixing the argument
Treating the stripped read as a copy edit, when it is a test of whether there is a claim at all
mobileRules: No mobile-specific behaviour; the stripped text is width independent
accessibilityRules: A page that reads correctly as plain text is close to what a screen reader user receives, which makes this a useful accessibility check as a side effect
genericnessNote: The test surfaces missing substance and prescribes nothing visual.

userJob: Verify what a page actually shows before reporting on it
problem: The page is assessed from its source or from a text dump, so hidden elements, clipped text and collapsed regions are reported as present and correct
worksWhen: Any claim about what a built page shows, at any point in the run
avoidWhen: Never; a host with no browser is a stated degraded mode, not an exemption
mechanism: Render the page and look at it, at the widths that matter, before saying what is on it. A markdown or text dump cannot see a hidden element, a zero-height container or a clipped line. Screenshots at 375, 768 and 1440, accessibility checks in both colour schemes, console errors, dead links and horizontal overflow are the evidence, and a build without them is reported as unverified rather than as passing.
risks: Reading a dump and reporting the DOM as the page
Capturing before the development server has compiled the route, which screenshots the compiler
mobileRules: 375px is captured as its own render, never inferred by narrowing the desktop screenshot mentally
accessibilityRules: Automated checks run in both light and dark schemes, because a contrast failure in one is invisible in the other
genericnessNote: A verification procedure constrains what may be claimed and nothing about the design.

userJob: Decide what to ask the client and when to stop asking
problem: Unknowns turn into a questionnaire, so the run stalls, or nothing is asked and the gaps become silent inventions
worksWhen: At the start of a build, after sorting the unknowns
avoidWhen: The brief already answers it, or the answer does not change what gets built
mechanism: Sort what you do not know into four piles: look it up, prototype it, assume it and say so, or ask. A pile becomes a question only if the brief is silent on it and the answer changes what gets built. One round, one question, with your default attached, asked as one open sentence. Silence means your default. Never ask what a thing should feel like; show two directions that differ in structure, or name two real pages and ask which is closer.
risks: Manufacturing a multiple-choice list of options you invented, which hands the client your defaults as if they were the field
Asking about taste, which produces an adjective and no decision
accessibilityRules: An accessibility constraint the client knows about is worth the one question, because assuming it is the expensive direction
genericnessNote: The question is derived from this brief's own silence, so it differs every time.
